newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan mulls economic zone for links with China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan mulls economic zone for links with China.

text.p: Taiwan said on Tuesday it may set up a special economic zone in its newly established offshore transshipment centre at Kaohsiung port, in a further step to extend shipping links with rival China.

"The ministry is considering creating an offshore economic zone or free zone at Kaohsiung where products will be allowed to be shipped directly to and from the mainland," Ting Chan-neng, a section chief with the transportation ministry, told Reuters.

Ting said the plan is an effort to boost the economic viability of Taiwan's newly established "offshore transshipment centre" at Kaohsiung -- designed to end a long-time ban on direct China-Taiwan shipping links.

Unlike the current scheme, which prohibits mainland goods from entering Taiwan customs, the proposed economic zone would allow semi-finished parts from the mainland to be processed at the Kaohsiung port, Ting said.
No schedule has been set for the implementation of the new zone, he said.
"We don't have a schedule for the economic zone. It will depend on demands for it," he said.
Products completed by factories in the economic zone would have to be sent back to China or a third country to ensure the processing remains an offshore matter.
"The entire process will be done offshore," Ting said.

Taiwan, which has banned direct links with China since 1949, has agreed to allow mainland cargoes to be shipped directly from China to Kaohsiung for onward passage to third countries as long as the cargoes do not enter Taiwan customs.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be put aboard ships planning to cross directly to the Chinese mainland.

Taiwan has said warmer Taipei-Beijing relations were needed before direct shipping, aviation and other links could begin. The two sides have been political rivals since they split after a civil war in 1949.
Transportation minister Tsai Jaw-yang on Tuesday urged China to open more ports to launch transshipment businesses due to the small size of the two current ports -- Xiamen and Fuzhou.
"Xiamen and Fuzhou are only capable of handing small volumes (of cargoes). We hope the mainland will open more ports," Tsai said.
Analysts estimate that Xiamen and Fuzhou ports have a combined cargo capacity of 100,000 20-foot equivalent units (TEU) -- tiny compared to the annual five million TEU handled by Kaohsiung.

Taiwan's private companies, which have invested a total of more than US$30 billion in China since a political thaw began in the 1980s, have pressed Taipei to completely lift the ban, saying direct links would benefit the island's economy.

The China-owned, St. Vincent-registered vessel Sheng Da made an historic voyage to Kaohsiung on Saturday, ending a 48-year impasse across the Taiwan strait. Another China-owned ship reached Kaohsiung on Sunday.
A Taiwan ship owned by the island's Uniglory Marine was scheduled to sail Xiamen on Thursday.
Analysts have said the transshipment exchanges carried more political significance than economic value.
